title: Acute bronchitis – Definition
content: Acute bronchitis is a type of chest infection.

title: Acute bronchitis – Definition
content: Acute bronchitis is usually self-limiting in nature.

title: Acute bronchitis – Pathophysiology
content: Acute bronchitis is a result of inflammation of the trachea.

title: Acute bronchitis – Pathophysiology
content: Acute bronchitis is a result of inflammation of the major bronchi.

title: Acute bronchitis – Pathophysiology
content: Acute bronchitis is associated with oedematous large airways.

title: Acute bronchitis – Pathophysiology
content: Acute bronchitis is associated with the production of sputum.

title: Acute bronchitis – Prognosis
content: The disease course of acute bronchitis usually resolves before 3 weeks.

title: Acute bronchitis – Prognosis
content: 25% of patients with acute bronchitis will still have a cough beyond 3 weeks.

title: Acute bronchitis – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: Viral infection is the leading cause of acute bronchitis.

title: Acute bronchitis – Epidemiology
content: Around 80% of acute bronchitis episodes occur in autumn or winter.

title: Acute bronchitis – Clinical features
content: Patients with acute bronchitis typically present with acute onset cough.

title: Acute bronchitis – Clinical features
content: The cough in acute bronchitis may or may not be productive.

title: Acute bronchitis – Clinical features
content: Patients with acute bronchitis typically present with acute onset sore throat.

title: Acute bronchitis – Clinical features
content: Patients with acute bronchitis typically present with acute onset rhinorrhoea.

title: Acute bronchitis – Clinical features
content: Patients with acute bronchitis typically present with acute onset wheeze.

title: Acute bronchitis – Clinical features
content: The majority of patients with acute bronchitis have a normal chest examination.

title: Acute bronchitis – Clinical features
content: Some patients with acute bronchitis may present with low-grade fever.

title: Acute bronchitis – Clinical features
content: Some patients with acute bronchitis may present with wheeze on examination.

title: Acute bronchitis – Differential diagnosis
content: Sputum, wheeze, breathlessness may be absent in acute bronchitis, whereas at least one tends to be present in pneumonia.

title: Acute bronchitis – Differential diagnosis
content: No other focal chest signs (dullness to percussion, crepitations, bronchial breathing) are present in acute bronchitis other than wheeze.

title: Acute bronchitis – Differential diagnosis
content: Systemic features (malaise, myalgia, and fever) may be absent in acute bronchitis, whereas they tend to be present in pneumonia.

title: Acute bronchitis – Investigations
content: Acute bronchitis is typically a clinical diagnosis.

title: Acute bronchitis – Investigations
content: If CRP testing is available, it may be used to guide whether antibiotic therapy is indicated for acute bronchitis.

title: Acute bronchitis – Management
content: Management of acute bronchitis includes analgesia.

title: Acute bronchitis – Management
content: Management of acute bronchitis includes good fluid intake.

title: Acute bronchitis – Management
content: Consider antibiotic therapy for acute bronchitis if patients are systemically very unwell.

title: Acute bronchitis – Management
content: Consider antibiotic therapy for acute bronchitis if patients have pre-existing co-morbidities.

title: Acute bronchitis – Management
content: Consider antibiotic therapy for acute bronchitis if patients have a CRP of 20-100mg/L (offer delayed prescription).

title: Acute bronchitis – Management
content: Consider antibiotic therapy for acute bronchitis if patients have a CRP >100mg/L (offer antibiotics immediately).

title: Acute bronchitis – Management
content: The BNF currently recommends doxycycline first-line for acute bronchitis.

title: Acute bronchitis – Management
content: Doxycycline cannot be used in children or pregnant women for acute bronchitis.

title: Acute bronchitis – Management
content: Alternatives to doxycycline for acute bronchitis include amoxicillin.

title: Allergic rhinitis – Definition
content: Allergic rhinitis is an inflammatory disorder of the nose where the nose become sensitized to allergens such as house dust mites and grass, tree and weed pollens.

title: Allergic rhinitis – Classification
content: Allergic rhinitis may be classified as seasonal.

title: Allergic rhinitis – Seasonal Rhinitis
content: Seasonal rhinitis occurs around the same time every year.

title: Allergic rhinitis – Hay Fever
content: Seasonal rhinitis which occurs secondary to pollens is known as hay fever.

title: Allergic rhinitis – Perennial Rhinitis
content: Perennial rhinitis symptoms occur throughout the year.

title: Allergic rhinitis – Occupational Rhinitis
content: Occupational rhinitis symptoms follow exposure to particular allergens within the work place.

title: Allergic rhinitis – Clinical features
content: Features of allergic rhinitis include sneezing.

title: Allergic rhinitis – Clinical features
content: Features of allergic rhinitis include bilateral nasal obstruction.

title: Allergic rhinitis – Clinical features
content: Features of allergic rhinitis include clear nasal discharge.

title: Allergic rhinitis – Clinical features
content: Features of allergic rhinitis include post-nasal drip.

title: Allergic rhinitis – Clinical features
content: Features of allergic rhinitis include nasal pruritus.

title: Allergic rhinitis – Management
content: Management of allergic rhinitis includes allergen avoidance.

title: Allergic rhinitis – Management
content: For mild-to-moderate intermittent, or mild persistent symptoms of allergic rhinitis, oral or intranasal antihistamines are used.

title: Allergic rhinitis – Management
content: For moderate-to-severe persistent symptoms of allergic rhinitis, or if initial drug treatment is ineffective, intranasal corticosteroids are used.

title: Allergic rhinitis – Management
content: A short course of oral corticosteroids are occasionally needed to cover important life events for allergic rhinitis.

title: Allergic rhinitis – Management
content: There may be a role for short courses of topical nasal decongestants (e.g. oxymetazoline) in allergic rhinitis.

title: Allergic rhinitis – Management
content: Topical nasal decongestants should not be used for prolonged periods as increasing doses are required to achieve the same effect (tachyphylaxis) and rebound hypertrophy of the nasal mucosa (rhinitis medicamentosa) may occur upon withdrawal.

title: Allergy tests – Skin prick test
content: The skin prick test is the most commonly used allergy test as it is easy to perform and inexpensive.

title: Allergy tests – Skin prick test procedure
content: In a skin prick test, drops of diluted allergen are placed on the skin after which the skin is pierced using a needle.

title: Allergy tests – Skin prick test capacity
content: A large number of allergens can be tested in one skin prick test session.

title: Allergy tests – Skin prick test controls
content: A skin prick test normally includes a histamine (positive) and sterile water (negative) control.

title: Allergy tests – Skin prick test results
content: A wheal will typically develop if a patient has an allergy in a skin prick test.

title: Allergy tests – Skin prick test interpretation time
content: Skin prick test results can be interpreted after 15 minutes.

title: Allergy tests – Skin prick test utility
content: Skin prick tests are useful for food allergies and also pollen allergies.

title: Allergy tests – Radioallergosorbent test (RAST)
content: The Radioallergosorbent test (RAST) determines the amount of IgE that reacts specifically with suspected or known allergens, for example IgE to egg protein.

title: Allergy tests – RAST results
content: RAST results are given in grades from 0 (negative) to 6 (strongly positive).

title: Allergy tests – RAST utility
content: RAST is useful for food allergies, inhaled allergens (e.g. Pollen) and wasp/bee venom.

title: Allergy tests – Blood tests
content: Blood tests may be used when skin prick tests are not suitable, for example if there is extensive eczema or if the patient is taking antihistamines.

title: Allergy tests – Skin patch testing
content: Skin patch testing is useful for contact dermatitis.

title: Allergy tests – Skin patch testing procedure
content: Around 30-40 allergens are placed on the back for skin patch testing.

title: Allergy tests – Skin patch testing irritants
content: Irritants may also be tested for in skin patch testing.

title: Allergy tests – Skin patch testing results
content: The patches are removed 48 hours later with the results being read by a dermatologist after a further 48 hours.

title: Cow's milk protein intolerance/allergy – Epidemiology
content: Cow's milk protein intolerance/allergy (CMPI/CMPA) occurs in around 3-6% of all children.

title: Cow's milk protein intolerance/allergy – Presentation time
content: CMPI/CMPA typically presents in the first 3 months of life in formula-fed infants.

title: Cow's milk protein intolerance/allergy – Presentation in breastfed infants
content: CMPI/CMPA is rarely seen in exclusively breastfed infants.

title: Cow's milk protein intolerance/allergy – Types of reactions
content: Both immediate (IgE mediated) and delayed (non-IgE mediated) reactions are seen in CMPI/CMPA.

title: Cow's milk protein intolerance/allergy – Terminology
content: The term CMPA is usually used for immediate reactions and CMPI for mild-moderate delayed reactions.

title: Cow's milk protein intolerance/allergy – Clinical features
content: Features of CMPI/CMPA include regurgitation and vomiting.

title: Cow's milk protein intolerance/allergy – Clinical features
content: Features of CMPI/CMPA include diarrhoea.

title: Cow's milk protein intolerance/allergy – Clinical features
content: Features of CMPI/CMPA include urticaria.

title: Cow's milk protein intolerance/allergy – Clinical features
content: Features of CMPI/CMPA include atopic eczema.

title: Cow's milk protein intolerance/allergy – Clinical features
content: Features of CMPI/CMPA include 'colic' symptoms: irritability, crying.

title: Cow's milk protein intolerance/allergy – Clinical features
content: Features of CMPI/CMPA include wheeze.

title: Cow's milk protein intolerance/allergy – Clinical features
content: Features of CMPI/CMPA include chronic cough.

title: Cow's milk protein intolerance/allergy – Complications
content: Rarely angioedema and anaphylaxis may occur in CMPI/CMPA.

title: Cow's milk protein intolerance/allergy – Diagnosis
content: Diagnosis of CMPI/CMPA is often clinical (e.g. improvement with cow's milk protein elimination).

title: Cow's milk protein intolerance/allergy – Investigations
content: Investigations for CMPI/CMPA include skin prick/patch testing.

title: Cow's milk protein intolerance/allergy – Investigations
content: Investigations for CMPI/CMPA include total IgE and specific IgE (RAST) for cow's milk protein.

title: Cow's milk protein intolerance/allergy – Management (severe symptoms)
content: If CMPI/CMPA symptoms are severe (e.g. failure to thrive) refer to a paediatrician.

title: Cow's milk protein intolerance/allergy – Management (formula-fed, mild-moderate)
content: For formula-fed infants with mild-moderate CMPI/CMPA symptoms, extensive hydrolysed formula (eHF) milk is the first-line replacement formula.

title: Cow's milk protein intolerance/allergy – Management (formula-fed, severe or no response)
content: For infants with severe CMPA or if no response to eHF, amino acid-based formula (AAF) is used.

title: Cow's milk protein intolerance/allergy – Soya intolerance
content: Around 10% of infants with CMPI/CMPA are also intolerant to soya milk.

title: Cow's milk protein intolerance/allergy – Management (breastfed)
content: If breastfed, continue breastfeeding for CMPI/CMPA.

title: Cow's milk protein intolerance/allergy – Management (breastfed maternal diet)
content: For breastfed infants with CMPI/CMPA, eliminate cow's milk protein from maternal diet.

title: Cow's milk protein intolerance/allergy – Management (breastfed maternal supplements)
content: Consider prescribing calcium supplements for breastfeeding mothers whose babies have, or are suspected to have, CMPI, to prevent deficiency whilst they exclude dairy from their diet.

title: Cow's milk protein intolerance/allergy – Management (breastfed, after stopping)
content: Use eHF milk when breastfeeding stops, until 12 months of age and at least for 6 months.

title: Cow's milk protein intolerance/allergy – Prognosis
content: CMPI usually resolves in most children.

title: Cow's milk protein intolerance/allergy – Prognosis (IgE mediated)
content: In children with IgE mediated intolerance, around 55% will be milk tolerant by the age of 5 years.

title: Cow's milk protein intolerance/allergy – Prognosis (non-IgE mediated)
content: In children with non-IgE mediated intolerance, most children will be milk tolerant by the age of 3 years.

title: Cow's milk protein intolerance/allergy – Challenge
content: A challenge is often performed in the hospital setting as anaphylaxis can occur.

title: Food allergy in children and young people – NICE guidelines
content: The 2011 NICE guidelines differentiate between IgE mediated and non-IgE mediated allergies.

title: Food allergy in children and young people – Food intolerance
content: The NICE guidance does not govern food intolerance, which is not caused by immune system dysfunction.

title: Food allergy in children and young people – First step
content: The first step is to identify possible food allergy and differentiate the possible causes: IgE-mediated and Non-IgE-mediated.

title: Food allergy in children and young people – IgE-mediated skin symptoms
content: IgE-mediated food allergy skin symptoms include pruritus, erythema, urticaria, and angioedema.

title: Food allergy in children and young people – Non-IgE-mediated skin symptoms
content: Non-IgE-mediated food allergy skin symptoms include pruritus and atopic eczema.

title: Food allergy in children and young people – IgE-mediated gastrointestinal symptoms
content: IgE-mediated food allergy gastrointestinal symptoms include nausea, gastro-oesophageal reflux, colicky abdominal pain, vomiting, and diarrhoea.

title: Food allergy in children and young people – Non-IgE-mediated gastrointestinal symptoms
content: Non-IgE-mediated food allergy gastrointestinal symptoms include loose or frequent stools, blood and/or mucus in stools, abdominal pain, infantile colic, food refusal or aversion, constipation, and perianal redness.

title: Food allergy in children and young people – IgE-mediated respiratory symptoms
content: IgE-mediated food allergy respiratory symptoms include upper respiratory tract symptoms (nasal itching, sneezing, rhinorrhoea or congestion with or without conjunctivitis) and lower respiratory tract symptoms (cough, chest tightness, wheezing or shortness of breath).

title: Food allergy in children and young people – Non-IgE-mediated other symptoms
content: Non-IgE-mediated food allergy other symptoms include pallor, tiredness, and faltering growth plus one or more gastrointestinal symptoms above (with or without significant atopic eczema).

title: Food allergy in children and young people – Symptoms of anaphylaxis
content: Symptoms of anaphylaxis are mentioned in the context of food allergy.

title: Food allergy in children and young people – Investigations (IgE-mediated)
content: If the history is suggestive of an IgE-mediated allergy, offer a skin prick test or blood tests for specific IgE antibodies to the suspected foods and likely co-allergens.

title: Food allergy in children and young people – Management (non-IgE-mediated)
content: If the history is suggestive of a non-IgE-mediated allergy, eliminate the suspected allergen for 2-6 weeks, then reintroduce.

title: Food allergy in children and young people – Dietitian consultation
content: NICE advise to 'consult a dietitian with appropriate competencies about nutritional adequacies, timings and follow-up' for non-IgE-mediated food allergies.

title: Latex allergy – Type I hypersensitivity
content: Sensitivity to latex may cause type I hypersensitivity (anaphylaxis).

title: Latex allergy – Type IV hypersensitivity
content: Sensitivity to latex may cause type IV hypersensitivity (allergic contact dermatitis).

title: Latex allergy – Irritant contact dermatitis
content: Sensitivity to latex may cause irritant contact dermatitis.

title: Latex allergy – Risk factors
content: Latex allergy is more common in children with myelomeningocele spina bifida.

title: Latex-fruit syndrome – Association
content: Many people who are allergic to latex are also allergic to fruits, particularly banana, pineapple, avocado, chestnut, kiwi fruit, mango, passion fruit and strawberry.

title: Oral allergy syndrome – Definition
content: Oral allergy syndrome, also known as pollen-food allergy, is an IgE-mediated hypersensitivity reaction to specific raw, plant-based foods including fruits, vegetables, nuts and certain spices.

title: Oral allergy syndrome – Clinical features
content: Oral allergy syndrome typically presents with mild tingling or pruritus of the lips, tongue and mouth.

title: Oral allergy syndrome – Pathophysiology
content: This hypersensitivity reaction is initiated by cross-reaction with a non-food allergen, most commonly birch pollen whereby the protein in the food is similar but not identical in structure to the original allergen.

title: Oral allergy syndrome – Association with pollen allergies
content: OAS is strongly linked with pollen allergies and presents with seasonal variation.

title: Oral allergy syndrome – Effect of cooking
content: Cooking culprit food, and thereby denaturing the proteins, prevents symptoms occurring in OAS.

title: Oral allergy syndrome vs food allergies – Cause
content: A food allergy is caused by direct sensitivity to a protein present in food. OAS is caused by cross-sensitisation to a structurally similar allergen present in pollen.

title: Oral allergy syndrome vs food allergies – Non-plant foods
content: Non-plant foods do not cause OAS because there are no cross-reactive allergens in pollen which would be structurally similar to meat.

title: Oral allergy syndrome vs food allergies – Stability of allergens
content: Food allergies may be caused by plant or non-plant foods and allergens occur in response to substances that are more stable and able to survive stomach enzymes and acid processing and cooking.

title: Oral allergy syndrome vs food allergies – Systemic symptoms and anaphylaxis
content: Food allergies are more likely to cause systemic symptoms (vomiting and diarrhoea) and are more likely to lead to anaphylaxis because the allergens are not readily broken down.

title: Oral allergy syndrome vs food allergies – OAS symptom limitation
content: The symptoms of OAS are normally limited to the oropharynx because the proteins that cause the symptoms are denatured by stomach enzymes.

title: Oral allergy syndrome – Epidemiology
content: About 2% of the UK population has OAS but this is probably under-diagnosed.

title: Oral allergy syndrome – Prevalence in pollen allergy
content: About 1/2 of patients with a general pollen allergy and 3/4 of patients with an allergy to birch pollen (the most common allergen in the UK) report symptoms of OAS.

title: Oral allergy syndrome – Associations
content: OAS is associated with Birch pollen allergy (most common) and Rye grass pollen allergy.

title: Oral allergy syndrome – Association with Latex allergy
content: OAS is associated with Rubber latex allergy.

title: Oral allergy syndrome – Presentation suspicion
content: OAS should be suspected in a patient with a history of seasonal allergy symptoms (rhinitis, conjunctivitis and asthma) who present with symptoms minutes after eating a specific raw food.

title: Oral allergy syndrome – Most common symptoms
content: Itching and tingling of the lips, tongue and mouth are the most common symptoms of OAS.

title: Oral allergy syndrome – Mild swelling and redness
content: Mild swelling and redness of the lips, tongue and throat may occur in OAS.

title: Oral allergy syndrome – Severe cases
content: In severe cases of OAS, patients develop nausea and vomiting.

title: Oral allergy syndrome – Symptom resolution
content: OAS symptoms fully resolve within one hour of contact.

title: Oral allergy syndrome – Complications
content: Anaphylaxis is a very rare complication of OAS.

title: Oral allergy syndrome – Signs (between episodes)
content: Most patients will have no visible signs during or between episodes of OAS.

title: Oral allergy syndrome – Signs (visible)
content: Some patients may have visible swelling and redness of the lips, tongue and oral mucosa in OAS.

title: Oral allergy syndrome – Signs of anaphylaxis
content: Patients with anaphylaxis present with wheeze, hives, hypotension and collapse.

title: Oral allergy syndrome – Investigations (diagnosis)
content: OAS is a clinical diagnosis.

title: Oral allergy syndrome – Investigations (rule out/confirm)
content: Further tests can be used to rule out diagnoses such as food allergies and to confirm the diagnosis when the history is unclear.

title: Oral allergy syndrome – Investigations (standard tests)
content: Standard IgE RAST and skin prick testing may be performed to identify common allergens such as pollens which co-exist with OAS.

title: Oral allergy syndrome – Investigations (pollen allergies and associated foods)
content: Common pollen allergies have specific associated foods which cause OAS. For example, birch allergy is associated with sensitivity to, amongst others, carrot, parsley and spinach.

title: Oral allergy syndrome – Investigations (food-specific IgE testing)
content: Food-specific IgE testing for OAS is unreliable and rarely performed clinically because the food does not survive processing.

title: Oral allergy syndrome – Investigations (skin prick testing with culprit foods)
content: Skin prick testing with culprit foods is more commonly used for OAS.

title: Oral allergy syndrome – Investigations (positive skin prick test)
content: A positive skin prick test for OAS would cause a small, itchy lump to develop on the skin.

title: Oral allergy syndrome – Management (avoidance)
content: Avoidance of culprit foods is the only required modification for the vast majority of patients with OAS.

title: Oral allergy syndrome – Management (symptomatic)
content: If culprit food is eaten and symptoms develop, an oral antihistamine can be taken for OAS.

title: Oral allergy syndrome – Management (anaphylaxis)
content: If symptoms of anaphylaxis develop in OAS, an ambulance should be called.

title: Oral allergy syndrome – Management (anaphylaxis treatment)
content: Intramuscular adrenaline may be required for anaphylaxis in OAS.

title: Oral allergy syndrome – Management (cooked foods)
content: Patients should be informed that once cooked, culprit foods should not cause symptoms in OAS.

title: Penicillin allergy – Prevalence
content: Allergy to penicillin based antibiotics is common.

title: Penicillin allergy – Misdiagnosis
content: Many patients who report a penicillin allergy may be describing an intolerance/side-effects (e.g. diarrhoea) or a coincidental rash (e.g. amoxicillin in patients with infectious mononucleosis).

title: Penicillin allergy – Cross-reactivity with cephalosporins
content: Around 0.5-6.5% of patients who are allergic to penicillin are also allergic to cephalosporins.

title: Penicillin allergy – BNF guidance on cephalosporins
content: The principal side-effect of the cephalosporins is hypersensitivity and about 0.5-6.5% of penicillin-sensitive patients will also be allergic to the cephalosporins.

title: Penicillin allergy – BNF guidance (immediate hypersensitivity)
content: Patients with a history of immediate hypersensitivity to penicillin should not receive a cephalosporin.

title: Penicillin allergy – BNF guidance (essential cephalosporin)
content: If a cephalosporin is essential in penicillin-allergic patients because a suitable alternative antibacterial is not available, then cefixime, cefotaxime, ceftazidime, ceftriaxone, or cefuroxime can be used with caution.

title: Penicillin allergy – BNF guidance (cephalosporins to avoid)
content: Cefaclor, cefadroxil, cefalexin, cefradine, and ceftaroline fosamil should be avoided in penicillin-allergic patients if a cephalosporin is essential.

title: Penicillin allergy – Types of penicillin
content: It is important to be aware of other types of penicillin and their trade names to avoid accidental prescription.

title: Penicillin allergy – Examples of penicillin types
content: Types of penicillin include phenoxymethylpenicillin, benzylpenicillin, flucloxacillin, amoxicillin, ampicillin, co-amoxiclav (Augmentin), co-fluampicil (Magnapen), piperacillin with tazobactam (Tazocin), and ticarcillin with clavulanic acid (Timentin).

title: Venom allergy – Classification of reactions
content: Allergic reactions to venom may be broadly considered as either local or systemic.

title: Venom allergy – Local reactions definition
content: Redness, swelling and pain limited to the skin and soft tissues directly related to the site of venom exposure, but spreading >10 cm from the site may be defined as 'local' reactions.

title: Venom allergy – Systemic reactions definition
content: Systemic reactions may refer to cutaneous reactions that are relatively distant from the exposure site e.g. widespread redness, itching, urticaria and/or angioedema (not affecting the mouth or throat).

title: Venom allergy – Anaphylaxis management
content: Anaphylaxis may occur with or without evidence of systemic cutaneous reaction and any reaction in which there is any airway compromise or signs and symptoms of haemodynamic compromise should be managed as anaphylactic in nature.

title: Venom allergy – Acute phase management
content: Broadly speaking, the management of venom allergy in the acute phase is supportive.

title: Venom allergy – Anaphylaxis treatment
content: Anaphylaxis should be managed with intramuscular adrenaline, intravenous steroids and intravenous anti-histamines as required.

title: Venom allergy – Anaphylaxis additional treatment
content: Oxygen and nebulised bronchodilators may also be required for anaphylaxis.

title: Venom allergy – Referral to allergy specialist
content: People who've had a systemic reaction to an insect bite should be referred to an allergy specialist.

title: Venom allergy – Testing recommendation (systemic reaction)
content: Testing for venom allergy is recommended in any patient with a history of a systemic reaction causing airway compromise or haemodynamic instability.

title: Venom allergy – Testing recommendation (systemic cutaneous reaction)
content: Testing for venom allergy may also be beneficial in patients with a history of a systemic cutaneous reaction where the allergen is felt to be difficult to avoid e.g. an allergy to bee stings in a beekeeper.

title: Venom allergy – Self-management plan
content: Patients with a history of a systemic reaction should be provided with a self-management plan, including guidance on the use of anti-histamines and adrenaline auto-injectors.

title: Venom allergy – Medical alert device
content: Patients should also be advised to wear a medical alert device for venom allergy.

title: Venom allergy – Venom immunotherapy (VIT)
content: Venom immunotherapy (VIT) is considered to be one of the most effective immunotherapies in use.

title: Venom allergy – VIT recommendation criteria
content: VIT may be recommended for patients with a history of a previous reaction which presented with airway and/or haemodynamic compromise and raised levels of venom-specific immunoglobulin E on either skin prick or in vitro testing.

title: Venom allergy – BSACI guidance on VIT contraindications
content: The British Society for Allergy and Clinical Immunology guidance advises that VIT should not be performed in patients without demonstrable venom-specific IgE or in those with a recent history of anaphylaxis or systemic reaction.

title: Venom allergy – Repeat allergy testing
content: Repeat allergy testing should be considered in those with a clear reaction history but no evidence of a venom-specific IgE.

title: Venom allergy – Baseline tryptase level
content: A baseline tryptase level should also be performed to exclude indolent mastocytosis (relevant because this may predict subsequent systemic reactions during the course of immunotherapy).

title: Asbestos-related lung disease – Overview
content: Asbestos can cause a variety of lung diseases from benign pleural plaques to mesothelioma.

title: Pleural plaques – Definition
content: Pleural plaques are benign and do not undergo malignant change.

title: Pleural plaques – Management
content: They, therefore don't require any follow-up.

title: Pleural plaques – Epidemiology
content: They are the most common form of asbestos-related lung disease and generally occur after a latent period of 20-40 years.

title: Diffuse pleural thickening – Aetiology
content: Asbestos exposure may cause diffuse pleural thickening in a similar pattern to that seen following an empyema or haemothorax.

title: Diffuse pleural thickening – Clinical features
content: This may be associated with a restrictive deficit on spirometry.

title: Asbestosis – Definition
content: Asbestosis is the name given to the lung fibrosis caused by asbestos.

title: Asbestosis – Pathophysiology
content: It is a lower lobe fibrosis.

title: Asbestosis – Complications
content: Patients are at increased risk of developing lung cancer (the risk is synergistic with smoking).

title: Mesothelioma – Definition
content: Mesothelioma is a malignant disease of the pleura.

title: Mesothelioma – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: There is a strong link with asbestos exposure (especially crocidolite, 'blue' asbestos).

title: Mesothelioma – Epidemiology
content: The latent period between exposure and disease is typically 30-40 years.

title: Mesothelioma – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: Workers who smoke and are exposed to asbestos have a much greater risk of lung cancer but not of mesothelioma.

title: Mesothelioma – Clinical features
content: Features progressive shortness-of-breath chest pain pleural effusion

title: Mesothelioma – Investigations
content: CXR: pleural effusion, pleural thickening

title: Mesothelioma – Investigations
content: pleural fluid is often blood-stained

title: Mesothelioma – Investigations
content: pleural biopsy is required for diagnosis

title: Mesothelioma – Management
content: chemotherapy radiotherapy supportive care

title: Mesothelioma – Prognosis
content: very poor, median survival is 8-14 months

title: Asthma – Definition
content: Asthma is a common chronic inflammatory disease of the airways characterised by variable and recurring symptoms, reversible airflow obstruction, and bronchospasm.

title: Asthma – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: Asthma is thought to be caused by a combination of genetic and environmental factors.

title: Asthma – Clinical features
content: Features of asthma include worsening dyspnoea, wheeze and cough that is not responding to salbutamol.

title: Asthma – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: Asthma symptoms may be triggered by a respiratory tract infection.

title: Asthma – Management
content: NICE updated their asthma guidelines in 2017.

title: Asthma – Management
content: The key change in NICE 2017 guidelines is a move away from recommending a salbutamol inhaler as the first step for adults with asthma.

title: Asthma – Management
content: NICE 2017 guidelines recommend a short-acting beta2-agonist (SABA) as a reliever therapy for all patients with asthma.

title: Asthma – Management
content: NICE 2017 guidelines recommend an inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) as the first-line preventer therapy for asthma.

title: Asthma – Management: Step 1
content: Step 1 of asthma management involves using a short-acting beta2-agonist (SABA) as required.

title: Asthma – Management: Step 2
content: Step 2 of asthma management involves adding an inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) at a low dose.

title: Asthma – Management: Step 3
content: Step 3 of asthma management involves adding a long-acting beta2-agonist (LABA).

title: Asthma – Management: Step 3 (LABA response)
content: If there is no response to LABA in Step 3, stop it and increase the ICS dose.

title: Asthma – Management: Step 3 (Inadequate control with LABA)
content: If there is benefit from LABA but control is still inadequate in Step 3, continue LABA and increase the ICS dose.

title: Asthma – Management: Step 4
content: Step 4 of asthma management involves considering increasing ICS to a high dose, or adding a fourth drug e.g. leukotriene receptor antagonist, theophylline.

title: Asthma – Management: Step 5
content: Step 5 of asthma management involves continuous use of oral steroids.

title: Bronchiolitis – Definition
content: Bronchiolitis is a common lung infection in young children and infants.

title: Bronchiolitis – Pathophysiology
content: Bronchiolitis causes inflammation and congestion in the small airways (bronchioles) of the lung.

title: Bronchiolitis – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: Bronchiolitis is almost always caused by a virus.

title: Bronchiolitis – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: The most common cause of Bronchiolitis is respiratory syncytial virus (RSV).

title: Bronchiolitis – Clinical features
content: Bronchiolitis features coryzal symptoms.

title: Bronchiolitis – Clinical features
content: Bronchiolitis features a dry cough.

title: Bronchiolitis – Clinical features
content: Bronchiolitis features increasing breathlessness.

title: Bronchiolitis – Clinical features
content: Bronchiolitis features wheezing.

title: Bronchiolitis – Clinical features
content: Bronchiolitis features low-grade fever.
